newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SWIMMING-GOLDEN ENCORE CHANCE FOR LE.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-GOLDEN ENCORE CHANCE FOR LE.

text.p: Olympic champion Le Jingyi aims for a unique third golden double this week in the world short-course championships, first global event since last year's Atlanta Games.
Le chases the 50 and 100 metres freestyle double she achieved in the inaugural short-course championships in Palma de Mallorca in 1993 and repeated in Rio de Janeiro in 1995.

The Chinese sprinter, who also won the two events at the 1994 world long-course championships in Rome and claimed the 100 freestyle gold in Atlanta, played down the significance of Gothenburg in a recent interview.
She said these championships would serve her as a warm-up for the Chinese National Games in Shanghai in October.
Nonetheless, she will be the swimmer to beat when she races the 100 on Thursday, first day of the four-day meeting, and the 50 on Friday.
In both events she faces a powerful challenge from Germany's Sandra Voelker, Olympic bronze medallist to Le's silver in the 50 and Olympic silver medallist to Le's gold in the 100.

Voelker won both the 50 and 100 freestyle, as well as the 50 backstroke, at last December's European short-course championships in Rostock, swimming within 0.03 of a second of Le's world record in the 100 freestyle.

Le's fellow Olympic champions Denis Pankratov and Claudia Poll share the spotlight in the Scandinavium indoor arena where a 25-metre stainless steel tank weighing 1,000 tons has been specially erected.
More than 700 competitors from 75 nations have entered the 32-event meeting as swimmers face a dramatically expanding championship calendar.
From now on there will be world championships every year to claim their attention, even in Olympic years.

The International Amateur Swimming Federation (FINA) Bureau decided on Monday to stage the long-course world championships every two years, instead of every four years, to run as frequently as the world short-course championships.

Next January's long-course championships in Perth, Australia, will be followed by short-course world championships in 1999 and 2000 and long-course in 2001. From then on the two will run in alternate years.
These third world short-course championships are the biggest so far, the first in Palma having attracted 46 nations and the second in Rio 56.

Pankratov, 100 and 200 metres butterfly champion at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, seeks to repeat that double in Gothenburg where his opponents include Australian Scott Goodman, winner of the 200 in Rio in the Russian's absence.
Poll, the Costa Rican who upstaged Germany's Franziska van Almsick to win the 200 metres freestyle in Atlanta, defends the 200 and 400 freestyle she won in Rio.

Others seeking to retain titles include Le's Chinese compatriots Wang Yiwu (men's 200 breaststroke) and Liu Limin (women's 100 butterfly) and Brazilian freestylers Fernando Scherer and Gustavo Borges.

American Misty Hyman goes for a repeat gold in the women's 100 backstroke and also contests the 100 and 200 butterfly, having recently lost her world record in the shorter of the two races. Compatriot Amanda Beard, double silver medallist in Atlanta, contests the two breaststroke events.

Organisers say that the day after the championships end, the pool's 92,500 litres of water will be drained into a nearby waterway and the tank dismantled to leave the arena clear for an international horse show later this month.

Before that happens, Uganda hope their whole team -- both of them -- will have had the chance to compete. The female member of the two-stong squad -- Joy N'Fashinggabo -- went missing at the airport before the flight from Entebbe and team officials have no idea where she is.
